Avanam Books: Deciding What Release 5.0 Will Not Do

A decision case on goals and non-goals in a product requirements document

1. Opening

At 7.40 on the morning of Monday 19 October 2026, Idhayavalli Pidugu opened the fifth draft of a document she had started two weeks earlier and found that it had grown again. As Head of Product at Avanam, in Chennai, she owed the leadership team a product requirements document for release 5.0 at their review on Friday 23 October. Building would start on Monday 26 October, and the release was due on Monday 14 December. Draft v5 held eight work items, with three more requests waiting in the comments. It had four paragraphs of goals and no section saying what the release would not do. She had until Friday to decide what to send, and what to write down as out.

2. Company background

Avanam, founded in Chennai in 2018, sells Avanam Books, a GST invoicing and bookkeeping app for small traders and manufacturers in Tiruppur, Coimbatore, Surat and Ludhiana. It has 38,000 paying merchants on an annual subscription of ₹4,800, which makes annual recurring revenue of ₹18.24 crore. Of these, 31,000 file a GSTR-3B return every month. Avanam competes with Vyapar and Zoho Books on software, with Tally Prime on the habits of merchants' accountants, and with Khatabook for the shop-counter ledger.

The 5.0 squad has six engineers, three in Bengaluru and three in Pune. A designer works from Berlin, a data scientist from Toronto, a customer-success lead from Singapore and the head of sales from New Jersey. The largest single customer is a trading group in Dubai.

3. The situation

Release 5.0 exists to fix one chore. A merchant can claim input tax credit only on purchase invoices that the supplier has reported, and the tax portal lists these each month in a statement called GSTR-2B. Merchants match their purchase books against it by hand. In September the Toronto data scientist timed 40 merchants: the median reconciliation took 95 minutes, and the nine merchants with more than one GSTIN took a median of 160. The goal Idhayavalli wrote in draft v1 was that by the GSTR-3B deadline of Wednesday 20 January 2027, 9,300 of the 31,000 monthly filers (30 per cent) would complete a reconciliation inside the app, with a median under 30 minutes.

The draft then moved. Between 5 and 16 October four requests from customer success went in one by one, as Exhibit 3 shows. Exhibit 2 lists every item and the engineer-weeks estimated for it, and Exhibit 1 sets out how many engineer-weeks the squad has. Diwali, on Sunday 8 November, closes the offices from Friday 6 to Tuesday 10 November. The Berlin designer had told Idhayavalli that each added item meant new screens, and that he had stopped reviewing after v3. Friday's review is at 6.30 pm IST, which is 3 pm in Berlin, 9 am in New Jersey, 5 pm in Dubai and 9 pm in Singapore.

4. The people

Inbamani Pemmaraju, Engineering Manager in Pune, leads the six-person squad. He wants the scope fixed on Friday, because after last quarter's incidents he holds 20 per cent of the squad's time for production support and will not give it up to a new feature.

Indukala Pulijala, Head of Sales in New Jersey, owns the Dubai group's renewal on Wednesday 31 March 2027. The group has 1,100 paid dealer seats at the list price of ₹4,800, which is ₹52.8 lakh a year, or about 2.9 per cent of recurring revenue. Its finance team has asked for invoices carrying UAE VAT, and she wants that in 5.0.

Isaivani Pasumarthi, Customer-Success Lead in Singapore, tags every support ticket by request. She brings the ranked list of what merchants ask for and wants the most requested items built first: WhatsApp payment reminders, Tally import and Hindi and Tamil screens.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 turns the squad into engineer-weeks, and Exhibit 2 prices the work asked of it, using a request tag customer success has applied since January 2026. Exhibit 3 plots each draft's total against the capacity in Exhibit 1, and Figure 1 puts the dates on a line.

6. The options

Option A: narrow the scope and write the exclusions down. Release 5.0 holds the core and the multi-GSTIN view, 25.5 engineer-weeks. The PRD gains a non-goals section naming the other six items, 37.0 engineer-weeks in all, each with its requester, its reason and a date to reopen it: Friday 29 January 2027, after the January filing. Indukala would tell the Dubai group before 14 December that UAE VAT is not in 5.0. The plan uses 83.0 per cent of capacity and leaves 5.22 engineer-weeks.

Option B: keep draft v5 and buy capacity. Avanam engages three contract engineers through a Pune vendor from Monday 2 November, at ₹2.0 lakh per person-month for the 40 days to 11 December, or ₹8.0 lakh. Onboarding takes five working days, ending Wednesday 11 November, which leaves 22 productive days each, 13.2 engineer-weeks. Capacity becomes 43.92 against 38.0 committed. The 13.2 carries no support reserve, and the review time the squad's engineers spend on the contractors' code is not netted out, so 43.92 is an upper figure. The three requests outside v5, 24.5 engineer-weeks, stay unplaced.

Option C: two releases with dates promised. Release 5.0 on 14 December holds the core, WhatsApp reminders and Tally import, 29.5 engineer-weeks, which is 96.0 per cent of capacity with 1.22 left. Release 5.1 on Friday 26 February 2027 holds the multi-GSTIN view, Hindi and Tamil screens and UAE VAT, 19.5 engineer-weeks. E-way bill and inventory tracking, 13.5 engineer-weeks, carry no date. No capacity plan for December to February exists, and each date becomes a commitment to sales and to customer success.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what does draft v5 commit against the capacity of the 26 October to 11 December window, and what does Exhibit 3 show about how that commitment moved?
  2. Which of the seven requests in Exhibit 2 would you test against the goal in section 3, and what test would you apply to each?
  3. What would a written non-goal need to say for Inbamani Pemmaraju and Indukala Pulijala each to treat it as binding?
  4. Which option would you take to Friday's review, and what would you say to the Dubai group?

8. A note for the learner

A goal says what success is. A non-goal says which plausible, wanted work the release will not do, and it earns its place by naming something a sensible person asked for. "No scope creep" is a hope, not a non-goal. A usable one has four parts: the item, the person who asked, the reason it is out, and the condition and date at which it comes back. Without the last two it reads as a refusal, and refusals get relitigated.

A well-reasoned answer does three things in order. It does the arithmetic before it argues. It applies one test to every request: does this item shorten the 95 and 160 minutes, or raise the number of merchants who complete a reconciliation by 20 January? And it gives each exclusion an owner who will say it aloud to the requester.

One defensible path is Option A. The core and the multi-GSTIN view pass the test: the first is the reconciliation, and the second acts on the nine merchants who took a median of 160 minutes. The other six address collections, migration, language reach, the Gulf, transport and stock, real problems but different goals. The PRD should hold the 5.22 spare engineer-weeks as contingency and say they are not an allowance for a non-goal.

The Dubai group is the hard conversation, and the dates make it manageable. At the squad's 4.8 engineer-weeks per calendar week (six engineers at 80 per cent), UAE VAT is about 2.3 weeks of work. If it is reopened on 29 January and a free squad needs a full three weeks from Monday 1 February, it lands around 19 February, more than five weeks before 31 March. Indukala can tell the group that UAE VAT is declined for 5.0 and will be decided on 29 January against the January data, and the same words go into the PRD.

Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Bahuroop Systems and the Field 3.0 Non-Goals

Chennai · Sunday, 11 October 2026

1 · The night beforeBesant Nagar, 9.40 p.m.

The north-east monsoon had come in over Chennai that afternoon and had not let up. On Joshitha Rajadurai's dining table in Besant Nagar lay three printed documents, and she had been moving between them since seven.

The first was the product requirements document for Bahuroop Field 3.0, ratified on Friday, 14 March 2025; its fourth section, headed Non-goals, ran to five sentences and she had drafted four of them. The second was the statement of work for Buhayra Retail Group of Dubai, signed on Monday, 2 February 2026 — at ₹9.60 crore of annual recurring revenue the largest contract Bahuroop Systems had signed. The third was a static scan of the Field codebase, run on Monday, 28 September 2026, counting twenty-nine places where behaviour depended on which tenant was asking.

At 9.30 next morning the roadmap council would sit, nine people across four time zones, to settle the January release; the board's product review followed on Tuesday, 20 October. In a notebook she had shown nobody, Joshitha had written a sentence she could not finish: the non-goals section was supposed to be the cheapest thing in the document, and instead it has cost us…

2 · Company historyOne binary, written in 2021

Bahuroop Systems Private Limited was founded in Chennai in 2019 by Jaivanth Rathinakumar and a classmate who left in 2022. Their first customer was a gold-loan NBFC whose officers photographed collateral where the network dropped for hours. Bahuroop Field — an application that renders a form from a specification and holds the result until it can sync — is still the only revenue-earning product.

In November 2021 the founders took the architectural decision that governs this case. Field would interpret its form specification entirely on the handset, with no server call in the capture path, and one binary reading one shared multi-tenant schema would serve every tenant. The bet paid twice: the app worked where competitors' did not, and the cost of adding a tenant fell to that of a configuration file. It also made two things expensive: logic that must look across records has nowhere to run, and data that must stay inside one country has nowhere to sit, because the schema is shared.

A ₹46 crore Series A followed in January 2023 and a ₹210 crore Series B in August 2025. At 30 September 2026 it employed 186 people, 74 of them in engineering and 7 in design. Cash stood at ₹168 crore against net burn of ₹4.20 crore a month, a runway of 40 months, and the board had asked for cash-flow breakeven in FY28.

3 · The industryWhere the scope pressure comes from

Field operations software in India is contested from three directions: the global suites, Salesforce Field Service and ServiceNow, bought when a parent group has standardised on them; the configurable application platforms, Zoho Creator foremost, which a competent analyst can bend into a field app in a fortnight; and the systems integrators, Infosys and TCS, who build bespoke against a tender and hand over the source.

Bahuroop sells against all three on one claim: the capture works when the network does not. Its demand sits in four regulated pockets — NBFC field verification, where the Reserve Bank's conduct expectations push lenders to evidence every field contact; insurance survey work under IRDAI's turnaround-time norms; retail and quick-commerce shelf audits, which grew fastest after Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart pushed dark-store compliance onto brand partners; and energy and utilities rounds, which came in with the solar build-out. Exhibit 1 sizes the four. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has made consent capture a contractual item in every renewal, and Bahuroop's compliance committee has set 31 March 2027 for its consent rework. Outside India, the United Arab Emirates' federal personal-data law and Saudi Arabia's PDPL have made in-country residency a procurement checkbox for Gulf retail groups — which is how a non-goal written in Chennai came to be read in Dubai in February 2026.

4 · The situation in detailWhat was believed, and what has turned out otherwise

The Field 3.0 document was ratified on 14 March 2025, the third marker in Figure 1, and its non-goals section passed without dissent: five sentences, each with a named owner, signed by Jaivanth. The minutes record the belief that the hard part had been writing them down. Exhibit 2 records what followed; nine of its eleven grants were taken a single agenda item at a time, and the minutes show none of those items running past ten minutes.

The second belief concerned residency. When Buhayra made in-country data a condition in January 2026, the answer was a UAE read replica, approved on 2 February 2026 as an exception to NG-2 and minuted as reporting only — understood in Chennai to mean a monthly pack. An August 2026 query census found that of 18.40 lakh queries in the month, 13.06 lakh — 71.0 per cent — came from Buhayra's store operations console, read by store managers the same day.

The third belief concerned where evaluation runs. In July 2026 Buhayra asked for an audit score computed across a store's previous four visits. NG-1 forbade server-side evaluation of form logic, so engineering built validation webhooks: at submit time Field calls an endpoint the tenant operates, and that server returns the score. The design note records NG-1 as honoured. Two things have since been measured. Bahuroop holds, per tenant, the ordering and retry semantics of those calls; and the call cannot run offline, so in September 2026 3,168 of Buhayra's 46,500 visits — 6.8 per cent — closed without a score.

The fourth belief was that one binary still served everyone. The scan of 28 September 2026 found 29 conditional branches keyed to tenant identifier, four tenants on divergent build flags, and only 6 of the 29 branches traceable to a granted exception. A joint session on 1 October tried to reconcile the 29 against the 62 behaviours in the commitments sheet; Exhibit 5 shows how far it got. On 6 October Buhayra's programme office wrote citing clause 4.3 of the February statement of work, which provides for “a composite audit score at point of capture, available offline”. Nobody in product had read clause 4.3 before signature; it was drafted in Iselin and reviewed in Singapore.

5 · The peopleEight positions, eight incentives

Joshitha Rajadurai — head of product, Chennai, since April 2024; joined January 2023. She drafted four of the five non-goals and holds that the register is the company's only instrument for a line. Incentive: the 20 October review is the first at which product owns the roadmap. Not saying: for two of the four build flags she wrote the register entry herself, after the build had shipped.

Jaivanth Rathinakumar — co-founder and chief executive, Chennai. He wants Buhayra intact through the Series C conversations he expects early in 2027, and has told two all-hands that Bahuroop will not become a no-code platform. Incentive: Buhayra is the Gulf reference the Series C narrative needs, and the not-a-platform line is what the Series B deck promised. Not saying: he has verbally agreed Phase 2 will be delivered.

Jenaka Ravipudi — vice-president, engineering, Bengaluru, since September 2024; 74 engineers, 17 on the Field platform squad. She commissioned the scan and wants the count, not the commitments sheet, treated as the measure of drift. Incentive: the sustaining load in Exhibit 4a. Not saying: two of the four divergent builds she authorised herself, before any exception was raised, to stop a renewal slipping.

Janmesh Rachamallu — principal engineer, platform, Pune; author of the interpreter and the only person on it since 2021. He argues that the webhook path has already produced what NG-1 was written to prevent. Incentive: one evaluation model, whichever side it runs on. Not saying: he holds an undecided offer from a Pune payments company.

Jemini Rajamani — senior product designer, Berlin; sole designer on Field Studio, the tenant administrator's builder. Her position: scope crept in the interface, not the codebase — Studio exposes eleven conditional block types and three more behind a feature flag. Incentive: a design system she can maintain alone across a shrinking daily overlap with Pune. Not saying: she has stopped documenting the hidden three.

Jigeeshu Rayachoti — data scientist, Toronto; owns platform telemetry. He produced the September split in Exhibit 4b and will not characterise it beyond the arithmetic. Incentive: telemetry as the shared instrument rather than three teams' spreadsheets. Not saying: his series breaks in April 2026, before which a build flag cannot be told from a configuration change.

Janvitha Ramasubbu — director, customer success, Singapore; owns the 23 managed-service tenants. She maintains the commitments sheet and argues that a promise to a tenant is scope whether or not it reached the codebase. Incentive: nine of her 23 accounts renew before 31 March 2027. Not saying: she co-reviewed clause 4.3 and never escalated it.

Jaytirth Raghupathy — head of sales, Americas and Gulf, Iselin, New Jersey, since June 2025; base USD 210,000, carried at ₹88 to the dollar. He wants cross-record rules declared a goal, and drafted clause 4.3. Incentive: a quota counting Gulf expansion at full value. Not saying: two of the five Gulf opportunities in Exhibit 6 have been told the capability exists.

7 · VoicesThe week of 5 October, in the team's own words

“The scan says twenty-nine, whatever anybody promised anybody. Four tenants are on their own build and thirty-seven are not, and I can give you the commit for each of the four.”

Jenaka Ravipudi, roadmap council minutes, Monday 5 October 2026, 09.40 IST

Janmesh Rachamallu, platform channel, Tuesday 6 October 2026, 23.14 IST

“Fourteen crore of next year's ARR turns on cross-record rules, and the Gulf is half of it. On capacity: we have two hundred and seventy-two engineer-weeks before the Dubai milestone. The ninety-six fits. This is not a resourcing argument, it is a willingness argument.”

Jaytirth Raghupathy, email to Joshitha and Jaivanth, Tuesday 6 October 2026, 10.12 EDT (19.42 IST)

“One hundred and sixty-two incidents in six months, forty-eight of them divergence. That is the platform's incident load, and my renewals are reading it. Whatever Monday decides, I need a sentence for nine accounts.”

Janvitha Ramasubbu, customer-success channel, Wednesday 7 October 2026, 08.05 SGT (05.35 IST)

“z is 3.93, so the gap between the two rows is outside sampling noise. I will not say more than that from this table. The four in the top row are also the four with the deepest specifications, and the flags went out on commercial request.”

Jigeeshu Rayachoti, telemetry note, Friday 9 October 2026, 07.20 EDT (16.50 IST)

8 · The optionsAs Joshitha sees them on Sunday night

Option 1 — Re-ratify the five non-goals unchanged

The five sentences stand as written in March 2025 and the five open requests are closed as refused. The 15 unaccounted promises in Exhibit 5, and the three unbuilt commitments touching NG-1, are withdrawn in writing. Cost: 22 person-weeks to unwind the webhook ordering layer, and Buhayra Phase 2 reduced by the clause 4.3 item, on which service credits of 2 per cent of the audit module's ₹2.80 crore annual fee — ₹5.60 lakh a week of slip — accrue to a 15 per cent cap, ₹42.00 lakh, after seven and a half weeks; a termination-for-convenience right opens on 31 March 2027 if Phase 2 is not accepted.

Option 2 — Delete NG-1 and build the rules engine as a goal

Cross-record evaluation becomes a first-class capability: a server-side evaluator, a versioned rule language, and an offline-evaluable subset for the capture path. NG-2 to NG-5 stand as written. Cost: 96 person-weeks inside the window of Exhibit 3, and nine further Studio block types, which Jemini costs at one designer for two quarters.

Option 3 — Keep NG-1 and publish a bounded extension contract

NG-1 stays in the register, and beside it Bahuroop publishes a supported tenant-extension contract: the validation-webhook path becomes a documented, versioned, synchronously called extension point with a declared latency budget, a stated offline fallback, and a quarterly budget of four exception grants. The 23 branches with no granted exception stay in place. Cost: 61 person-weeks, 18 of them documentation, conformance tests and a certification harness.

Option 4 — Split the product line

A second tier, Field Enterprise, is created in which per-tenant logic and per-country residency are goals rather than exceptions, metered and priced separately; the core product keeps all five non-goals and the common binary, and the four tenants on divergent build flags, Buhayra among them, move across. Cost: 34 person-weeks for packaging and migration; a tier-wide hiring ask of 6 engineers at a loaded ₹33.30 lakh each, ₹2.00 crore a year across the four tenants; and a Buhayra-only UAE residency stack at ₹1.42 crore a year — ₹84 lakh of cloud, 1.5 site-reliability engineers at ₹49.95 lakh in all, ₹8 lakh of audit. Against a Buhayra gross profit of ₹6.82 crore at the 71 per cent blended margin the stack alone leaves ₹5.40 crore, or 56.2 per cent of the ₹9.60 crore, before any share of the ₹2.00 crore; charged the whole of it, ₹3.40 crore, or 35.4 per cent.

Joshitha had written the four on one page in that order, and under them two notes she had shown nobody: which of these does the register actually do?, and clause 4.3 was drafted in Iselin, reviewed in Singapore, signed in Chennai.

9 · The deadline and the hard constraints

The roadmap council sits at 9.30 IST on Monday, 12 October 2026 — 06.00 in Berlin, 00.00 in Iselin and Toronto, 12.00 in Singapore — and its output is the January release scope; the board's product review follows on 20 October. Buhayra Phase 2 acceptance falls on 31 January 2027 and requires a production release, which must land in one of the 11 release weeks Exhibit 3 leaves.

Money and people are fixed inside the window. Exhibit 3's 68 uncommitted person-weeks are the whole of the platform squad's free capacity, and the board's engineering headcount cap of 74 holds until the first quarter of FY28, so any hiring is a board item on 20 October. The DPDP consent rework carries a 31 March 2027 date. Janmesh has worked on the interpreter continuously since 2021; Jemini is the only designer on Studio, and Berlin runs three and a half hours behind Chennai until 25 October and four and a half after it.

Shortly before eleven Joshitha opened the governance tracker and scrolled to the bottom. The last entry was dated 19 August 2026 and the owner field held her predecessor's name. The rain had got into the balcony and she went to shut the door. On the table the three documents lay as she had set them down at seven: March 2025, February 2026, September 2026.

10 · Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 records nineteen exception requests against five written non-goals, eleven granted. On that evidence, what did the Field 3.0 non-goals section bind, and whom?
  2. Exhibit 5 sets three counts beside one another: 62, 29 and 11. Reconcile them as far as the data allows, and say what the roadmap council would need to know before adopting any of them as its measure.
  3. Exhibit 1 shows annual revenue per field user running from ₹4,684 in NBFC field verification to ₹23,301 at Buhayra. What does that range imply about whose requirements should set the platform's scope, and what does Exhibit 1 not tell you?
  4. Exhibit 3 leaves 68 uncommitted person-weeks before 31 January 2027. For each option in section 8, what would have to be surrendered, by whom, and on whose authority?
  5. Clause 4.3 of the 2 February 2026 statement of work promises a composite audit score at point of capture; NG-1 of the 14 March 2025 PRD forbids server-side evaluation of form logic. Do the two conflict? If they do, which should govern, who should own it next time, and what would have to change for your answer to hold without Joshitha's personal intervention?
  6. What should Joshitha do on the morning of Monday, 12 October, and what should she say to the board on 20 October when it asks whether writing the non-goals down changed anything?
exp20v2-req.goals.nongoals:
Goals and Non-Goals

What are we deliberately not doing, and have we written it down?

1. Twelve weeks, five engineers, four requests

On Monday 9 March 2026, Pavneet Aneja, a senior product manager at Halwara Fleet, a Ludhiana software company whose app helps road-transport operators track trucks and close out driver accounts, had twelve weeks, five engineers and one condition. A Jalandhar transporter running 310 trucks had agreed a ₹96 lakh annual contract, provided the new trip-settlement module went live by Monday 1 June. Settlement means reconciling a driver's cash advance against the fuel, toll and repair receipts he brings back from a trip. At the transporter it took 6.5 days on average, and drivers waited for their balance.

Her inbox held four further requests. Prabhjot Atri, head of sales, wanted Punjabi and Hindi screens. The transporter's operations lead wanted a link to the e-way bill, the electronic permit that GST rules require for goods moving by road. Halwara's finance team wanted fuel-card reconciliation, and the owner wanted a dashboard. Each came from someone entitled to ask, and each was defensible. Palvinder Abrol, the engineering lead, had told her he would build whatever the product requirements document (PRD) said on Friday 13 March, and whatever was added afterwards too. That, he said, was the difficulty. The previous release had shipped nine weeks late after its scope grew by a third, and nobody could point to the day it happened.

If she wrote the PRD as a list of what to build, every later request would arrive as a small addition to an unfinished list. If she also wrote down what the team would not build, and why, each later request would have to argue against a document. Missing 1 June meant losing the ₹96 lakh contract and a reference customer in the Punjab transport corridor. The decision on 13 March was therefore how the document would handle the four requests.

2. The idea: a goal is a commitment, a non-goal is a refusal

A goal states an outcome the work must achieve and the measure that will show it did. A non-goal is something a reasonable person could want from this work that the team has chosen, in writing, not to deliver. Both halves matter, and the second is harder: nobody is embarrassed to leave things unwritten, so they stay unwritten.

The problem it solves is scope creep, the accumulation of individually sensible additions. Each costs a few days and each has a champion, and the champion pays nothing; the schedule pays. Project management has long listed exclusions in its scope statements, and engineering teams turned the pairing into a standard heading. Malte Ubl's 2020 description of design documents at Google is the clearest account: non-goals are not negated goals. "The system should not crash" is a non-goal only in the grammatical sense, because nobody wants a crash. A true non-goal is something that could plausibly have been a goal.

The sentence Pavneet could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "These are good ideas, they are not what this release is for, and here is what would make us reconsider."

3. How it works: seven steps, four of them usually implicit

First, write the goals, ranked, each with a measure. Pavneet's three were: drivers record advances and expenses on a phone, even offline; a branch manager settles a trip within one working day; and the ledger exports to the transporter's accounting software. A non-goal is only meaningful against a goal, since it is the goal that makes an addition irrelevant.

Second, collect every candidate ask, including those no one has voiced. This is the first implicit step. Creep lives in unspoken expectations, so she asked each stakeholder what they assumed would be in. Third, test each ask against the goals: does it serve one? Fourth, price it in engineer-days and compare with capacity (the next section).

Fifth, for each exclusion name who bears the cost and what would reopen the question. That trigger is what turns a refusal into a decision rather than a veto. Sixth, have the people excluded read the list and say they understand; silence is not agreement. Seventh, treat the document as a gate. Every late request is run through step 3 again, in public, against the same text.

At Halwara, step five produced the dashboard line. The owner would read the ledger export instead, and the cost to him was a spreadsheet filter. Step six meant sending the draft to all five people it affected on 11 March, two days before the review, and asking each for objections in writing.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic

Capacity first. Five engineers working twelve five-day weeks supply 300 engineer-days. Leave, reviews, support and meetings remove some, so a yield factor applies. Halwara's planning convention was 0.8. A fifth of what remains is held as contingency. The rest is plannable. Her goals cost 62 days (offline entry), 58 (approval workflow) and 44 (ledger export), totalling 164. The four requests cost Punjabi and Hindi screens 30, fuel-card reconciliation 45, e-way bill link 35 and dashboard 25, totalling 135.

Pass 1 already shows that accepting everything overruns by 107 days, 56 per cent of plannable capacity (107 ÷ 192). Pass 2 changes one input. Palvinder pulled the last two releases' actual yields, 0.72 and 0.68, a mean of 0.70. Plannable capacity falls to 168, headroom to four days, and the overrun to 131. One input moved by an eighth, and the room for anything beyond the goals nearly vanished.

Notice what pass 1 shows. The 25-day dashboard fits inside 28 days of headroom, yet it serves no goal. Capacity is a constraint, not the criterion, which is why she tested goals before pricing. She wrote the list on pass 2.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

A non-goal is not a negated goal.

"Do not lose data" excludes nothing anyone proposed. If no stakeholder could be disappointed by a line, it is decoration, and it crowds out lines that could.

A non-goal is not the backlog.

A backlog item has simply not been examined, while a non-goal has been examined and refused. Teams that merge the two stop being able to say which ideas were decided.

"Not now" and "never" are different promises.

Most non-goals are really deferrals and should say so, with a trigger. Calling a deferral "never" makes the next conversation a fight.

Capacity is not the test.

The dashboard fit. Using leftover room as the criterion turns the plan's only slack into someone else's feature, with the contingency next in line.

Someone pays, and the page should say who.

Declining Punjabi screens costs the sales team a talking point and perhaps drivers some comfort. A list that hides this will be reopened by the people who pay.

Slices are still scope.

"Just the CSV import" of a declined feature is a smaller version of the same decision. Price it, and compare it with headroom.

Written is not agreed.

A list nobody excluded has read is a private opinion. Circulate it, and ask for objections before the build starts rather than after.

What it cannot tell you.

The list cannot say whether the goals are right. A disciplined team can defend a wrong goal perfectly. Before relying on it, ask who disagrees with the goals, what evidence set the triggers, and who has read it.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In consumer products the pressure is diffuse: growth, design and executives each want an experiment, and a non-goal is mostly a defence of focus. In B2B it is concentrated. A single customer's contract can carry a feature, as the e-way bill link nearly did at Halwara, so the list must say whether a request is the customer's condition or merely their preference. In a marketplace the sharp question is which side a feature serves. Declining a buyer-side feature is a decision about suppliers too, and the page should name both.

Stage matters as much. A start-up of eight can enforce a non-goal by conversation, and the list is a memory aid. A large company has more requesters than the PM can reach, so the document must stand in for her. A buyer who asks for a feature in a 200-person company can usually be found and talked to; in a 20,000-person company, requests arrive through channels the PM cannot see. The same section is a courtesy in the first case and the main defence in the second.

7. Common mistakes

The list of the obvious. Symptom: non-goals such as "no security breaches" that nobody ever contests. Misunderstanding: that a long list shows rigour. Diagnostic: for each line, name the person who asked for the opposite. If no one can be named, delete it.

The undeclared price. Symptom: the section is reopened in week five by an angry sponsor who says they never agreed. Misunderstanding: that stating an exclusion is the same as obtaining consent. Diagnostic: ask each affected person to repeat what was excluded, in their own words.

The permanent maybe. Symptom: items marked "out of scope for now" with no date or condition, so every meeting retries them. Misunderstanding: that vagueness is diplomacy. Diagnostic: ask what single observation would move the item, and write it beside the line.

The goal-free list. Symptom: exclusions argued from taste or fatigue. Misunderstanding: that non-goals stand alone. Diagnostic: for each, name the goal it fails to serve.

8. What good looks like

By 1 June the Halwara list had met three tests, each handled in the document's own words. On Tuesday 7 April the transporter asked for the e-way bill link, and Pavneet pointed to the line, its trigger and the pilot review. On Tuesday 21 April Prabhjot Atri escalated the Punjabi screens. The line's trigger was a driver survey: if more than 25 per cent of sampled pilot drivers could not complete an entry unaided, the item would reopen. Halwara's field team sampled 120 drivers using the early offline-entry build, and 21 failed, which is 17.5 per cent. The trigger was not met, and Prabhjot accepted the number because he had agreed the test beforehand.

On Tuesday 12 May finance asked for only the CSV import of fuel-card reconciliation, 12 days. Against headroom of four it was eight days over, and the answer was no, with the written trigger of 31 July, sixty days after go-live. The module went live on Monday 1 June. Good is not an absence of requests. It is a record in which every request met a sentence written weeks before.

9. The decision, and what to carry forward

She chose to publish the four exclusions with the 0.7 numbers, though the 0.8 plan would have pleased the sponsors. Her reasoning: a list can be defended only if it is true, and a plan that required 0.8 would be reopened the first time yield dropped. She sent Palvinder the figures first so he could attack them; he found no error. She also kept the headroom of four days unallocated, because a plan with no slack turns every illness into a missed date.

What to learn next: how a PRD's goals receive their measures, because a non-goal is only as firm as the goal behind it; then prioritisation methods, which rank candidates but do not by themselves decline any.

Two questions to sit with. Think of a feature your team declined verbally: who would be surprised to learn it was declined, and why have they not been told? And which of your current goals could not be failed by any outcome, so that it excludes nothing?
exp40v2-req.goals.nongoals:
Goals and non-goals

On writing down what you are not doing, and why the best evidence for the practice does not clear its own noise.

1. Two decisions that look identical

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, in Gurugram, Rachana Bajwa had two spreadsheets open and one decision to make by Friday. Bajwa runs product at Inveka Systems, which sells a claims and revenue-cycle platform to Indian hospital chains and carries about ₹118 crore of recurring revenue. The first was the request ledger for Inveka's Q1 FY27 cycle: forty-six requests arrived after the PRD was signed on 24 March, eighteen were admitted, consuming 131 engineer-days, and a release promised for 30 June shipped on 11 August, forty-two days late.

The second spreadsheet was the cycle that followed. For Q2 FY27 Bajwa had done three things at once: fixed the ship date, instituted a quarterly sweep of standing exclusions, and put a six-line section headed Non-goals into the PRD. Forty-one requests arrived after sign-off and eleven were admitted, so the admitted share fell from 39 per cent to 27 per cent. Her engineering director, Rashika Birdi, had given her verdict on the inference: “You changed three things and one number moved.”

On Thursday 8 October, Ranjodh Behl was weighing a single sentence. Behl is head of product at Ilvara Instruments in Pune, which builds cold-chain loggers for pharmaceutical distribution: 18,400 Gen-1 units are in service across eleven distributor networks, and Gen-2 is planned at 42,000 units over twenty-four months against a programme budget of ₹4.60 crore. The first line under Non-goals read that Gen-2 would not provide real-time telemetry. Six of the seventeen distributors and prospects Ilvara interviewed had named real-time visibility unprompted, and his operations director, Raunaq Badhwar, wanted the line struck. The tooling order was due on Friday 30 October, and after it the enclosure and the radio were facts about the world.

The two decisions look alike. They are not, and the analytical content of this topic sits in the difference.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A goal is a committed outcome a team accepts being judged on. A non-goal is stranger than it appears: a written statement, in the specifying artefact, that a plausible adjacent outcome a stakeholder would assume is in scope will not be pursued in a named window, with the reason, the reopening condition, and the person who may overturn it. Four of the five are usually missing, and one missing them is a mood, not a decision. The negation is of an outcome, not a feature, and it comes from the narrow band of things that look included.

The vocabulary has two roots. The older is specification practice: the exclusions clause of defence specifications and the scope section of IEEE 830-style requirements documents, both written to stop an implementer elsewhere inferring scope from silence. The more influential root is the engineering design document, where the heading became conventional: the Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal template carries Goals and Non-Goals as adjacent mandatory fields. The intellectual root is Herbert Simon's 1955 point that a bounded agent cannot optimise every dimension at once, so every plan silently designates dimensions it will merely satisfice. The strategy literature arrives from the other side: a position is constituted by what it refuses.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic of a written exclusion

Experts do not start from the goals. They enumerate the candidate goal set, everything a stakeholder might believe is in, and sort it. Writing a line is neither free nor expensive, so it can be priced. Let A be the cost of settling a request mid-cycle, A′ the cost of settling it when a written non-goal exists, w the cost of writing and maintaining it, and p the probability per cycle that the request arrives. The line pays when p(A − A′) exceeds w.

Inveka had timed the terms. Across the fourteen Q1 requests the product manager time-logged, a contested request consumed a mean of 11.5 person-hours: 4.0 product manager, 3.0 engineering lead, 2.5 account team, 2.0 support. Across the nine Q2 requests that ran into a written non-goal the mean was 2.5, so A − A′ is 9.0 person-hours. Drafting a line with its reason, window and trigger took 0.75 person-hours including review, and re-examining it at the next two planning cycles 0.5 each, so w = 1.75 over a three-cycle life — 0.583 a cycle, which is the horizon p(A − A′) is measured on. The break-even probability is therefore 0.583 divided by 9.0, or 0.065: about one cycle in fifteen. Both means come from small unrandomised subsets, A is a Q1 figure and A′ a Q2 one, so the 9.0 carries the same three-way confound as section 10's admitted share, and neither mean has a recorded spread.

Two second-order effects follow. The first is that A′ is not a constant: it rises with list length, because a longer section is slower to search. At p = 1/9, the white-label edition's rate, the condition requires A − A′ above 0.583 divided by one-ninth, or 5.25 person-hours, so with A = 11.5 the line stops paying once A′ passes 6.25. Nobody has measured that slope, and it is the missing parameter on which the schools divide. The second effect runs the other way: writing an exclusion down advertises that the team has considered it, which may raise p. Inveka's account team was quoting the section to customers within three weeks, and one pair of cycles cannot recover that effect's sign.

One inference the ledger does not support: the 66-engineer-day overrun did not cause the forty-two-day slip in any arithmetic sense. Sixty-six engineer-days on a two-person critical path is about thirty-three working days each, call it seven calendar weeks; the release lost forty-two days, or thirty working days. The two are the same order and neither derives the other, because the queue was not shareable.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

State the conditions as testable claims. C1: there exist adjacent outcomes a reasonable stakeholder would assume are in scope. Ask three stakeholders to write the scope from memory and count disagreements; Inveka's forty-six post-signature requests and Ilvara's six of seventeen distributors and prospects both settle C1. C2: settling the argument mid-cycle costs materially more than settling it in writing in advance. Inveka observed that gap at 9.0 person-hours across two cycles; a team that has not measured it asserts C2 rather than testing it. C3: the exclusion is reversible at a cost you can price. C4: a named person may overturn it.

C3 separates the two protagonists and is most often waved through. Inveka's exclusions reverse on a smooth curve: the four admitted analytics requests cost 18 engineer-days together, 3.1 per cent of a quarter's gross capacity. Ilvara's reverses on a step function that jumps at the tooling order and never comes back down. Where C3 fails a non-goal is not a scope device but a bet, and should be written as one: a stated probability, a payoff, an owner who accepts both.

Where is the idea actively misleading? Three places. Where the excluded outcome is a legal obligation: Inveka cannot make conformance with the National Health Claims Exchange a non-goal, though it can make dental claims one for FY27, because jurisdiction is a scope choice and compliance is not. Where a team uses the heading to disclaim a floor. And pre-product-market-fit, where the job is to chase the request that arrives.

5. Hard edges, and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company the non-goal and the goal are often one sentence seen from two rooms. Inveka's claims product says payer-side analytics is out; the group's analytics unit says it is in; the hospital controller hears “no” from one and “soon” from the other. In two-sided businesses it is sharper: a supply-side exclusion degrades demand-side liquidity with a lag, so the team writing the non-goal is not the one whose metric carries the cost. The diagnostic is one question: whose number gets worse if we are right? An exclusion answering somebody else's is a transfer, not a decision.

Regulated products add an effect legal teams understand and product managers do not: a written non-goal is discoverable. In a dispute, “reconciliation of partially-settled claims is a non-goal” reads very differently to a regulator than in a sprint review, and the usual response, softening it to “not in the current release”, destroys the function while keeping the heading. AI-native products break the form itself: “the assistant will not give dosage advice” cannot be honoured by a sentence, because the system is a distribution, not a switch. It must become a measured refusal rate against a threshold on a named evaluation set — so the non-goal has turned into a non-functional requirement with a number in it.

What mature companies do rather than say: they say every PRD carries a non-goals section, and the sections exist. In practice the lines are copied forward unexamined, and what holds scope is headcount allocation plus a date somebody senior will be embarrassed to move. The written exclusion does real work only where a decision must survive a handoff to people who were not in the room.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The negation is of an outcome, never a feature. The tell is a list that reads like a backlog with “not” in front of each line. Feature negations get routed around: someone ships the capability under another name and the outcome arrives anyway. Specificity feels like rigour; here it buys precision in the wrong currency.

A window and a trigger, or it is a ratchet. The tell is a line surviving three consecutive PRD reviews uncommented. Exclusions decay towards permanence: arguing against a settled line costs the arguer and benefits nobody present. An unexamined non-goal is a liability, not discipline.

No named overturn authority means no decision. The tell is the same argument reopening at a different altitude each time: account team, engineering director, board deck. Escalation looks like healthy contest; it shows the exclusion never said who could end one.

“Performance is a non-goal” is almost always a disguised non-functional requirement. The tell is an exclusion with no number in it. Latency, uptime and data loss have floors you cannot declare away: a logger dropping excursion records is not descoped, it is defective. Write the floor and call it an NFR.

The section is a price list. The tell is a non-goal quoted back inside a customer's RFP response as “on the roadmap”. That looks like leakage to stop. In fact publication may raise the arrival rate, and one pair of cycles cannot show whether it did.

In enterprise software the exclusion is quasi-contractual. The tell is procurement asking for the non-goals list by name. Keep two registers: an internal one with reasons and triggers, an external one saying only what is not in the current release.

The exclusion that matters is usually a segment, not a feature. The tell is a team that can list the features it is not building but cannot name the customer it is not serving. Inveka's diagnostic-lab line may be worth more than the other five of its Q3 register together, because segments generate coherent products. Calling segment exclusions a strategy matter is how they go unwritten.

A non-goal binds only where an incentive agrees with it. The tell is that nobody's compensation gets worse when the line is violated. An expert reads the comp plan before the PRD, and treats a non-goal cutting against a commission accelerator as decorative until proven otherwise.

7. What actually differs by product type and stage

Less than the literature implies, and the differences are about enforcement rather than form: the five-field anatomy of Figure 3 does not change between them. Consumer teams rarely write non-goals and enforce exclusions by not instrumenting the thing. B2B and enterprise is where the artefact matters most. Platforms carry the cross-side externality; hardware carries irreversibility; AI products convert exclusions into thresholds.

By stage the pattern is cleaner. At seed the non-goals are the strategy and three verbal lines suffice. The practice pays most where headcount outruns shared memory, around Series B, where Inveka sits. At scale-up the ratchet appears and the sweep becomes the mechanism. In mature companies the register is a legal instrument.

8. Three worked examples

Inveka, the line that paid. Payer-side analytics arrived in nine of nine quarters, p = 1.00, far above the 0.065 break-even. The Q2 section carried it with a window to 31 March 2027, a reason class of sequencing, a trigger of two top-ten accounts naming it in a renewal, and Bajwa as overturn authority. Four of Q1's eleven analytics requests were admitted, at 18 engineer-days; in Q2, none. Had the line existed in Q1, the 9.0-hour saving across eleven conversations would have been about 99 person-hours against the 0.583 the line costs per cycle: the honest arithmetic, and the whole of the evidence.

Ilvara, the line priced as an option. Fitting the module now costs ₹780 per unit of incremental bill of materials, ₹327.6 lakh across the 42,000-unit plan. Keeping the option, by laying out a board and enclosure that accept it later, costs ₹94 lakh of non-recurring engineering: ₹224 per unit amortised across the full plan, or 28.7 per cent of the ₹780 to exercise. That ₹224 assumes the whole plan is built; at half the plan the premium doubles to ₹448.

Inveka, the line that failed. “Multi-entity consolidated reporting is a non-goal” entered a PRD on Monday 12 August 2024 with a reason but no window, trigger or owner, and three successive PRDs cited it as settled. By early 2026 seven of Inveka's twelve largest accounts had become multi-entity through hospital-chain consolidation: 58 per cent of a group that, as at 1 October 2025, contributed ₹41 crore of the company's ₹96 crore of ARR. Two of the seven did not renew, on 31 December 2025 and 31 January 2026, taking ₹6.2 crore of that ₹96 crore October 2025 book, 6.5 per cent. The line was right in August 2024 and wrong by mid-2025, and nobody had a reason to look. The recovery was the sweep of Figure 3: 23 lines examined, four promoted to goals, fourteen renewed with windows, five deleted.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each has a sign appearing before the cost does, and a question that surfaces it in a minute.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The specification school holds the list should be long and specific, its evidence Inveka's observed 9.0 person-hours per avoided argument: at that saving anything asked once in fifteen cycles earns a line. It is wrong if A′ rises steeply with list length, and nobody has measured that slope. The strategy school holds the list should be two or three lines or absent, its evidence the ratchet, and that a long register is how a team avoids writing a strategy. It is wrong if exclusions are mostly local and sequencing-driven rather than positional, which Inveka's ledger suggests: 25 of the 46 requests, 54 per cent, were sequencing or analytics matters.

The option-value school holds a non-goal should always be a deferral with a trigger, never a flat negation, and Ilvara's 28.7 per cent premium prices it. It is wrong if a deferral fails to end the argument the way a verdict does — plausible, and unmeasured.

The capacity school deserves most attention, because this page's best evidence cannot separate it from the practice. Inveka's admitted share fell from 18/46 = 0.391 to 11/41 = 0.268, a drop of 12.3 points. With a pooled proportion of 29/87 = 0.333, the standard error of the difference is √(0.333 × 0.667 × (1/46 + 1/41)) = 0.101, so the drop is 1.21 standard errors, a two-sided p near 0.22. It is not a finding. Worse, the arm is confounded: Bajwa fixed the date, started the sweep and added the section in one cycle, and the capacity school attributes the movement to the date. Detecting a 12.3-point difference at 80 per cent power and the 5 per cent threshold needs about (1.96 + 0.84)² × (0.238 + 0.196) ÷ 0.123², or 225 requests per arm: just over five ledgers each side, at Inveka's mean of 43.5 requests a ledger — and the two ledgers span twenty and fourteen weeks, so even that mean mixes unequal exposure. Birdi was right.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a non-goals section. Someone who has internalised it writes the exclusions before the goals; names a customer rather than a feature; puts a date and a named person on every line; prices the reversal before choosing the form, so an irreversible exclusion is written as a bet and a reversible one as a decision; refuses to declare a floor away; reads the compensation plan before believing any of it; and, asked for evidence that the practice works, says the observation is 9.0 person-hours per argument across two confounded cycles and the rest is inference. The last is rarest.

12. What they decided

Three questions first. Bajwa will not claim the twelve-point fall as evidence, so on what basis should she keep or drop the practice? Ilvara pays 28.7 per cent of the exercise price to keep its option open: at what probability of the request would you refuse to pay, and what does your answer imply about how many hardware exclusions should be decisions at all? And the break-even rule licenses a line for anything asked once in fifteen cycles, while the strategy school calls a register that long a confession: which position is making a claim that could be tested, and by what measurement?

Bajwa kept the section at six lines, each carrying all five fields, dropping the white-label edition — whose clearance of the break-even is inside its own standard error — for the thing the Q2 version lacked: the diagnostic-lab segment, named as a segment. She declined to put the admit-rate figure in the board pack, and asked Birdi to hold the ship-date discipline constant for five quarters. Behl struck the flat negation for a deferral: Gen-2 ships without telemetry, the modem-ready footprint is bought before 30 October, and the trigger is two of the top five distributors writing real-time visibility into a tender before 31 March 2027, with Badhwar holding authority to call it.

13. Going deeper

PRD structure is where the non-goals section lives; without it the exclusions have nothing to be exclusions from. PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc tells you which document an exclusion belongs in. Writing a one-pager forces the segment-level exclusion onto one page. Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N) surface the near-miss band. Acceptance criteria and error cases is the opposite discipline, bounding what counts as done. Telemetry requirements gives the observable a revisit trigger needs. Non-functional requirements is where disguised non-goals belong.
